text: 4 Lower Bound via Hidden Eigenbasis

The preprint [ 22 ] proved an $\Omega(\log d)$ query lower bound for centered Gaussian sampling with $I_{d}\preceq A\preceq 2I_{d}$ at total variation accuracy $\varepsilon=\frac{1}{10}$ . We subsequently examine the limitations of this analysis for establishing accuracy-dependent lower bounds in Section 4.4 .
Theorem 4.1 ( Extension to general $\kappa$ ).
For every fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$ , there exists $d_{0}(\delta)$ such that, for every integer $d\geq d_{0}(\delta)$ , $2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}$ , and $0<\varepsilon\leq 1/10$ ,
$Q_{G}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon)\geq\frac{\delta}{256}\sqrt{\kappa}\log d.$

Compared with Theorem 3.1 , this bound also covers $2\leq\kappa<4$ and $\frac{1}{16}<\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{10}$ , and it holds even when the spectrum of $A$ is known to the algorithm. On the other hand, it does not grow as $\varepsilon\to 0$ and it requires $\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}$ .
4.1 The Hard Family

We use a construction similar to that in [ 22 , Section 9.2] , with a cosine eigenvalue grid (Chebyshev nodes) and a random orthogonal rotation, while extending the spectral interval from $[1,2]$ to $[1,\kappa]$ . For $d\geq 2$ and $\kappa\geq 2$ , define
$\theta_{i}=\frac{(i-\tfrac{1}{2})\pi}{d},\qquad\lambda_{i}=\frac{\kappa+1}{2}+\frac{\kappa-1}{2}\cos\theta_{i},\qquad\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}).$ (11)

Draw $O\sim\operatorname{Haar}(\mathrm{O}(d))$ , independently of the algorithm’s private randomness, and set $A=O\Lambda O^{\top}$ . The associated potential and target are $f_{A}(x)=x^{\top}Ax/2$ and $\pi_{A}=N(0,A^{-1})$ .
The spectrum is deterministic and may be supplied to the algorithm. In particular, the Gaussian normalizing constant is known. The unknown component is the random eigenbasis represented by $O$ .
Remark 4.2 ( Comparison with $\kappa=2$ case).

At $\kappa=2$ , the spectrum in Eq. ( 11 ) recovers the original construction in [ 22 ] . More generally, if $A_{2}$ denotes the original precision matrix with the same rotation $O$ , then $A=(\kappa-1)A_{2}-(\kappa-2)I_{d}$ . Thus one matrix–vector reply for either matrix determines the corresponding reply for the other. The proof compares $\sum_{i}\cos(n\theta_{i})\langle x,Oe_{i}\rangle^{2}$ with $\|x\|^{2}$ , where $n=2q+1$ . For the output of a $q$ -query algorithm, the ratio is at most $d^{-\Omega(1)}$ in absolute value (Lemma 4.4 ), whereas under the target the ratio of the means has absolute value $e^{-\Theta(n/\sqrt{\kappa})}$ (Lemma 4.5 ). Hence the test works for $n$ up to order $\sqrt{\kappa}\log d$ , rather than $\log d$ as at $\kappa=2$ , which is the source of the factor $\sqrt{\kappa}$ in Theorem 4.1 .
4.2 Properties of the Hard Family

This subsection states the four lemmas used in the proof of Theorem 4.1 . Lemma 4.3 places the output of any $q$ -query algorithm in a block Krylov space generated by independent Gaussian vectors, Lemma 4.4 bounds a quadratic form with cosine weights uniformly over this space, Lemma 4.5 evaluates the same quadratic form under the target, and Lemma 4.6 verifies that the hard family is admissible. All proofs are deferred to Appendix C .
Krylov representation of the output.

We first control the information revealed by adaptive queries via a standard Krylov argument. The deferred-rotation argument of [ 22 , Lemma 9.2] uses the rotational symmetry of the undisclosed eigenbasis to represent the algorithm’s output in a block Krylov space generated by independent Gaussian vectors.
For vectors $g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d})$ , define
$\mathcal{K}_{q}(g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1})=\operatorname{span}\{\Lambda^{j}g_{a}:1\leq a\leq q+1,\ 0\leq j\leq q\}.$
Lemma 4.3 ( Krylov representation).
Fix an integer $q\geq 0$ with $2q+1<d$ and let $X$ be the output. There exist independent vectors $g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}\sim N(0,I_{d})$ such that
$O^{\top}X\in\mathcal{K}_{q}(g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1})\qquad\text{almost surely}.$

The additional starting vector accounts for the output, which may lie outside the span of the query points and oracle replies. Equivalently, the lemma gives a representation $O^{\top}X=\sum_{a=1}^{q+1}p_{a}(\Lambda)g_{a}$ , where each $p_{a}$ has degree at most $q$ . The polynomial coefficients may depend on the entire extended experiment. We therefore control the output through an estimate that holds simultaneously for every vector in $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ . The proof of Lemma 4.3 is deferred to Appendix C.1 .
A uniform bound on the Krylov space.
We next control a high-frequency cosine statistic uniformly over the space in Lemma 4.3 . For a query budget $q$ , set
$n=2q+1,\qquad D_{n}=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\cos(n\theta_{1}),\ldots,\cos(n\theta_{d})\bigr).$
The choice of $n$ places this statistic above all frequencies arising from products of two degree- $q$ cosine polynomials.
Lemma 4.4 ( Uniform bound on the Krylov space).

There is an absolute constant $C>0$ such that the following holds. Let $q\geq 0$ satisfy $2q+1<d$ , let $g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}$ be independent $N(0,I_{d})$ vectors, and let $\mathcal{K}_{q}=\mathcal{K}_{q}(g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1})$ . Define
$\tau_{d,q}=C\left[(q+1)\sqrt{\frac{\log d}{d}}+\frac{(q+1)(q+1+\log d)\log d}{d}\right].$
If $\tau_{d,q}\leq 1/2$ , then, with probability at least $0.99$ ,
$|u^{\top}D_{n}u|\leq 2\tau_{d,q}\|u\|^{2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal{K}_{q}.$

The proof is deferred to Appendix C.2 . Since $\lambda_{i}$ is a nonconstant affine function of $\cos\theta_{i}$ , the space $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ is equivalently spanned by the vectors $\bigl((g_{a})_{i}\cos(j\theta_{i})\bigr)_{i=1}^{d}$ , with $a\leq q+1$ and $j\leq q$ . Consequently, the estimate is independent of $\kappa$ .
On the event in Lemma 4.4 , the output representation in Lemma 4.3 therefore gives
$\bigl|X^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}X\bigr|\leq 2\tau_{d,q}\|X\|^{2}.$
Target moments.
We now evaluate the same cosine statistic under the target Gaussian.
Lemma 4.5 ( Moments under the target).

Let $\kappa\geq 2$ , $U\sim N(0,\Lambda^{-1})$ , and $\varrho_{\kappa}=\tfrac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}$ . For an integer $1\leq n<d$ , put $D_{n}=\operatorname{diag}(\cos(n\theta_{i}))$ , $M=\mathbb{E}\|U\|^{2}$ , and $\mu_{n}=\mathbb{E}[U^{\top}D_{n}U]$ . Then

$\displaystyle M$ $\displaystyle=\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\frac{1-\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d}}{1+\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d}},\quad\mbox{and }(-1)^{n}\mu_{n}=\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\frac{\varrho_{\kappa}^{n}-\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d-n}}{1+\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d}}.$
Moreover, both $\operatorname{Var}(\|U\|^{2})$ and $\operatorname{Var}(U^{\top}D_{n}U)$ are at most $2M\leq 2d/\sqrt{\kappa}$ .
If $d-n\geq\sqrt{\kappa}$ , then
$(1-e^{-4})e^{-3n/\sqrt{\kappa}}\leq\frac{|\mu_{n}|}{M}\leq e^{-2n/\sqrt{\kappa}}.$

The proof is deferred to Appendix C.3 . For an exact sample $Y\mid O\sim\pi_{A}$ , the vector $U=O^{\top}Y$ has law $N(0,\Lambda^{-1})$ , with $\|Y\|^{2}=\|U\|^{2}$ and $Y^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}Y=U^{\top}D_{n}U$ . The lemma therefore gives the means and variances of $\|Y\|^{2}$ and $Y^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}Y$ under the target.
Admissibility and oracle equivalence.
We finally verify that the hard family belongs to the prescribed class. The proof is deferred to Appendix C.4 .
Lemma 4.6 ( Admissibility).
For every $O\in\mathrm{O}(d)$ , the matrix $A=O\Lambda O^{\top}$ satisfies $I_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}$ .
4.3 Proof of Theorem 4.1
We compare the probabilities of a single test event under algorithmic outputs and target samples.
Proof of Theorem 4.1 .

Fix $\delta\in(0,1)$ , $2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}$ , and $0<\varepsilon\leq 1/10$ . Suppose that an algorithm uses at most $q\leq(\delta/256)\sqrt{\kappa}\log d$ queries and satisfies $\operatorname{TV}(\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}},\pi_{A})\leq\varepsilon$ for every admissible $A$ . Lemma 4.6 makes the hard family admissible.
Set $n=2q+1$ and $\tau=\tau_{d,q}$ . Define statistic $S_{A}$ and the associated test event $E_{A}$ as
$\displaystyle S_{A}(x)$ $\displaystyle:=(-1)^{n}x^{\top}T_{n}\!\left(\frac{2A-(\kappa+1)I_{d}}{\kappa-1}\right)x-2\tau\|x\|^{2},$
$\displaystyle E_{A}$ $\displaystyle:=\{x:S_{A}(x)>0\},$
where $T_{n}$ is the degree- $n$ Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind.

Geometrically, for $x\neq 0$ , the weights $w_{i}(x)=|\langle x,Oe_{i}\rangle|^{2}/\|x\|^{2}$ describe the fractions of its energy $\|x\|^{2}$ carried by the eigenvectors $Oe_{i}$ of $A$ . Using $T_{n}(\cos\theta_{i})=\cos(n\theta_{i})$ , the event $x\in E_{A}$ is equivalent to $(-1)^{n}\sum_{i}w_{i}(x)\cos(n\theta_{i})>2\tau$ . So $E_{A}$ is the event that the cosine coefficient $\sum_{i}w_{i}(x)\cos(n\theta_{i})$ of these weights at frequency $n$ exceeds $2\tau$ in absolute value and has the sign that it has under the target.
Algorithmic outputs rarely pass the test.
The bound on $q$ gives $q+1\leq d^{(1-\delta)/2}\log d$ , so $n=o(d)$ . Substituting this bound into the definition of $\tau$ yields
$\tau\lesssim d^{-\delta/2}(\log d)^{3/2}+d^{-\delta}(\log d)^{3}\lesssim d^{-\delta/2}(\log d)^{3}\longrightarrow 0$

Thus $n<d$ and $\tau\leq 1/2$ for sufficiently large $d$ depending only on $\delta$ , and the Lemma 4.3 and Lemma 4.4 apply. Let $X$ be the algorithmic output on the random input $A=O\Lambda O^{\top}$ . Lemma 4.3 places $O^{\top}X$ in $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ on an extension preserving the joint law of $(O,X)$ . Lemma 4.4 then gives
$|X^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}X|\leq 2\tau\|X\|^{2}$
with probability at least $0.99$ . On this event, $S_{A}(X)\leq 0$ . Consequently,
$\mathbb{E}_{A}[\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}(E_{A})]\leq 0.01.$
Target samples typically pass the test.

Let $M=\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda^{-1})$ denote the target mean squared norm, and let $\mu_{n}=\operatorname{tr}(D_{n}\Lambda^{-1})$ denote the target mean of the cosine statistic. Write $\beta=|\mu_{n}|/M$ for the normalized target bias.
Since $n=o(d)$ and $\sqrt{\kappa}\leq d^{(1-\delta)/2}=o(d)$ , we have $d-n\geq\sqrt{\kappa}$ for sufficiently large $d$ . Lemma 4.5 and the the bound on $q$ therefore give
$\beta\geq(1-e^{-4})e^{-3n/\sqrt{\kappa}}\geq b\,d^{-\delta/4},\qquad b=(1-e^{-4})e^{-3},$

where we used $3n/\sqrt{\kappa}\leq 3+(3\delta/128)\log d$ . Moreover, $\varrho_{\kappa}\leq e^{-1/\sqrt{\kappa}}$ and $d\geq\sqrt{\kappa}$ imply $\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d}\leq e^{-2}<1/3$ . The formula for $M$ in the same lemma yields $M\geq d/(2\sqrt{\kappa})\geq d^{(1+\delta)/2}/2$ . Together with the bound on $\tau$ above, these estimates imply
$\frac{\tau}{\beta}\leq\frac{C^{\prime}}{b}d^{-\delta/4}(\log d)^{3}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad M\beta^{2}\geq\frac{b^{2}}{2}\sqrt{d}\longrightarrow\infty.$

All estimates are uniform over the stated parameter range. We may therefore choose $d_{0}(\delta)$ so that the conditions for the algorithmic bound above hold and, additionally, $\tau\leq\beta/4$ and $M\beta^{2}\geq 320$ .

Now fix $A$ , draw $Y\sim\pi_{A}$ , and set $Z=S_{A}(Y)$ . Lemma 4.5 gives mean $(-1)^{n}\mu_{n}=\beta M$ for the signed cosine quadratic form and mean $M$ for $\|Y\|^{2}$ . Both variances are at most $2M$ . Hence, using the $L^{2}$ triangle inequality for centered variables,
$\mathbb{E}Z=(\beta-2\tau)M\geq\frac{\beta M}{2},\qquad\operatorname{Var}(Z)\leq\bigl(\sqrt{2M}+2\tau\sqrt{2M}\bigr)^{2}\leq 8M.$
Chebyshev’s inequality gives, for every $A$ in the hard family,
$\pi_{A}(E_{A})=\mathbb{P}(Z>0)\geq 1-\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Z)}{(\mathbb{E}Z)^{2}}\geq 1-\frac{32}{M\beta^{2}}\geq 0.9.$
Contradiction.
Finally, the per-input TV guarantee implies $\pi_{A}(E_{A})-\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}(E_{A})\leq\varepsilon$ . Averaging over the random input and using the two probability bounds gives
$0.89\leq\mathbb{E}_{A}\!\left[\pi_{A}(E_{A})-\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}(E_{A})\right]\leq\varepsilon\leq 0.1,$
a contradiction. ∎
4.4 Limitations of the Analysis

Theorem 4.1 is restricted to $2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}$ for fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$ . Although it applies to every $\varepsilon\leq 1/10$ , its lower bound does not grow as $\varepsilon$ decreases. We discuss two limitations of the analysis that affect extensions to larger condition numbers and higher accuracy.
Limitation on $\kappa$ .

Our approach does not extend the $\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ lower bound to condition numbers $\kappa\gtrsim d/\log^{2}d$ . Our proof controls the output of the algorithm by first applying Lemma 4.3 to place $O^{\top}X$ in $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ , and then bounding the cosine statistic uniformly over this space. However, the enlarged space $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ has $(q+1)^{2}$ generating vectors. Since the eigenvalues of $\Lambda$ are distinct, these vectors span a space of the following dimension.
Lemma 4.7 ( Dimension of the Krylov space).
For every integer $q\geq 0$ and independent $g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}\allowbreak\sim N(0,I_{d})$ ,
$\dim\mathcal{K}_{q}=\min\{d,(q+1)^{2}\}\qquad\text{almost surely}.$

Once $(q+1)^{2}\geq d$ with $q=\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ , we have $\mathcal{K}_{q}=\mathbb{R}^{d}$ almost surely. For $n=2q+1<d$ , the definition of $\theta_{i}$ gives $\sum_{i}^{d}\cos^{2}(n\theta_{i})=d/2$ , so at least one coordinate satisfies $|\cos(n\theta_{i})|\geq 1/\sqrt{2}$ . Taking its coordinate unit vector yields
$\sup_{u\in\mathcal{K}_{q}\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|u^{\top}D_{n}u|}{\|u\|^{2}}\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$

Our separating test in Lemma 4.4 requires this supremum to be at most $1/2$ , which is incompatible with the displayed bound. Thus an argument based on a uniform bound over $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ cannot apply once $(q+1)^{2}\geq d$ .
Limitation on accuracy.

Our test compares the ratio $(-1)^{n}x^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}x/\|x\|^{2}$ with a threshold $t$ . Lemma 4.4 puts every output of the algorithm below $t$ only if $t\geq a$ , where $a$ is the uniform bound on $\mathcal{K}_{q}$ that the lemma provides. Chebyshev’s inequality with Lemma 4.5 puts samples from the target above $t$ only if $t<|\mu_{n}|/M$ . Thus $|\mu_{n}|/M>a$ , whatever the threshold. At the same time, the Bernstein calculation in the proof of Fact C.6 requires $a\geq c/\sqrt{d}$ even to certify a failure probability below one. Finally, Lemma 4.5 gives $|\mu_{n}|/M\leq e^{-2n/\sqrt{\kappa}}$ . Since $n=2q+1$ , we must have
$\frac{c}{\sqrt{d}}\leq a<\frac{|\mu_{n}|}{M}\leq e^{-2(2q+1)/\sqrt{\kappa}}.$

Taking logarithms yields $q=O(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ , independently of $\varepsilon$ . A different choice of the threshold or of the constants therefore cannot give a bound that grows as $\varepsilon\to 0$ .
Remark 4.8 ( Scope of the limitations).

These limitations concern our proof. We do not know whether the same fixed-spectrum family supports stronger lower bounds. Our analysis therefore leaves open whether the same fixed-spectrum family supports stronger lower bounds.
